name: Rosa Parks
kicker: Civil rights activist · Her 1955 arrest sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott
briefing: On December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks, a 42-year-old seamstress and secretary of the local NAACP, refused a bus driver’s order to give up her seat to a white passenger in Montgomery, Alabama, and was arrested. Her arrest sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott, a 381-day protest led by a young Martin Luther King Jr. that ended after the courts struck down bus segregation. Congress later honored her as “the first lady of civil rights.”

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A few months before her most famous act, this woman attended a workshop on ending segregation at the Highlander Folk School in Tennessee. She had served for years as secretary of her city’s NAACP chapter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose arrest in Montgomery, Alabama, in December 1955 started a bus boycott.

tossups.p: In 1943, bus driver James F. Blake made this woman get off his bus so that she could re-enter through the back door, then drove away before she could get back on. She avoided riding his buses for years afterward.
tossups.r: In 1955, she refused Blake’s order to give up her seat. For 10 points, name this woman whose arrest led to the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

tossups.p: E. D. Nixon, a leader of the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, joined the white couple Clifford and Virginia Durr to bail this woman out of jail. Nixon believed her case was the right one to challenge her city’s segregated buses.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this seamstress whose arrest in Montgomery, Alabama, sparked a famous bus boycott.

tossups.p: Nine months before this woman’s arrest, a 15-year-old named Claudette Colvin was arrested for refusing to give up her seat on a bus in the same city. Colvin later became a plaintiff in _Browder v. Gayle_, the case that ended bus segregation there.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman who was arrested on a Montgomery bus on December 1, 1955.

tossups.p: Jo Ann Robinson and the Women’s Political Council stayed up all night printing leaflets after this woman’s arrest, calling on Black residents to stay off the buses on the day of her trial. That one-day protest grew into a boycott that lasted 381 days.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose refusal to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, made her a symbol of the civil rights movement.

tossups.p: The lawyer Fred Gray defended this woman after her arrest, then filed _Browder v. Gayle_ on behalf of four other women who had faced discrimination on city buses. In that case, a federal court ruled that bus segregation in this woman’s city was unconstitutional.
tossups.r: The Supreme Court upheld that ruling in 1956. For 10 points, name this woman whose arrest started the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

tossups.p: In 2013, this woman became the first Black woman honored with a full-length statue in the U.S. Capitol. When she died in 2005, she became the first woman to lie in honor in the Capitol Rotunda.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this civil rights activist who refused to give up her bus seat in 1955.

tossups.p: This woman worked in the Detroit office of Congressman John Conyers for more than twenty years, beginning in 1965. The Henry Ford Museum in nearby Dearborn displays the city bus from her most famous moment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose 1955 arrest in Montgomery, Alabama, led to a bus boycott.

tossups.p: This woman was riding the Cleveland Avenue bus home from her job as a seamstress at a department store when she made history. She later explained that she was not physically tired that evening: “the only tired I was, was tired of giving in.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose refusal to give up her seat sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

tossups.p: This woman, born with the last name McCauley in Tuskegee [“tuh-SKEE-gee”], Alabama, grew up on her grandparents’ farm in Pine Level. She married a barber named Raymond who was active in the NAACP.
tossups.r: She later became secretary of the NAACP’s Montgomery branch. For 10 points, name this woman who was arrested on a Montgomery bus in 1955.

tossups.p: On December 5, 1955, this woman was found guilty of breaking her city’s bus segregation law and fined ten dollars plus court costs. That same day, a new group called the Montgomery Improvement Association chose a young minister as its leader.
tossups.r: That minister was Martin Luther King Jr. For 10 points, name this woman whose arrest started the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

tossups.p: This woman received the NAACP’s Spingarn Medal in 1979, the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1996, and the Congressional Gold Medal in 1999. Congress also honored her as “the first lady of civil rights.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose arrest on a Montgomery bus in 1955 sparked a year-long boycott.

tossups.p: This woman wrote a 1992 autobiography with Jim Haskins and a 1994 book about her faith called _Quiet Strength_. She moved to Detroit in 1957 after losing her job and receiving threats in Alabama.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose refusal to give up her bus seat made her a symbol of the civil rights movement.

tossups.p: A well-known photograph of this woman being fingerprinted was actually taken in February 1956, when she and dozens of other boycott leaders were arrested under an old Alabama law against boycotts. Martin Luther King Jr. was also charged under that law.
tossups.r: Her first arrest had come months earlier on a city bus. For 10 points, name this woman whose arrest in December 1955 launched the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

tossups.p: In November 1956, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld a ruling against segregated buses in this woman’s city, and the boycott there ended about a month later. During that boycott, many Black residents walked or shared rides in carpools instead of riding the buses.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose refusal to give up her seat sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

clues.t: Refused to give up her bus seat to a white passenger in Montgomery, Alabama, on December 1, 1955, and was arrested
Her arrest sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–1956), led by Martin Luther King Jr.
Honored by Congress as “the first lady of civil rights” and “the mother of the freedom movement”
Secretary of the Montgomery branch of the NAACP
Said “the only tired I was, was tired of giving in”; she was not physically tired
The boycott lasted 381 days; many Black residents walked or carpooled instead of riding the buses
_Browder v. Gayle_ (1956) ruled Montgomery’s segregated buses unconstitutional, and the Supreme Court upheld it
Worked as a seamstress at the Montgomery Fair department store
Fifteen-year-old Claudette Colvin had refused to give up her seat nine months earlier
Moved to Detroit in 1957 and worked for Congressman John Conyers from 1965 to 1988
E. D. Nixon and Clifford and Virginia Durr bailed her out of jail
Jo Ann Robinson and the Women’s Political Council printed leaflets calling for the boycott
Driver James F. Blake ordered her to move; in 1943 he had driven off after making her get off to re-enter through the back door
Months before her arrest, attended a workshop on ending segregation at the Highlander Folk School in Tennessee
Was riding the Cleveland Avenue bus home from work
Lawyer Fred Gray defended her and filed _Browder v. Gayle_
_Browder v. Gayle_’s plaintiffs were Aurelia Browder, Susie McDonald, Claudette Colvin, and Mary Louise Smith, not her
Was convicted and fined $10 plus court costs on December 5, 1955, the first day of the boycott
Born Rosa Louise McCauley in Tuskegee, Alabama (1913); grew up on her grandparents’ farm in Pine Level
Her husband, Raymond, was a barber and an NAACP member
In 2005, became the first woman to lie in honor in the U.S. Capitol Rotunda
In 2013, became the first Black woman honored with a full-length statue in the U.S. Capitol
The bus from her arrest is displayed at the Henry Ford Museum in Dearborn, Michigan
Won the NAACP’s Spingarn Medal (1979), the Presidential Medal of Freedom (1996), and the Congressional Gold Medal (1999)
Wrote an autobiography with Jim Haskins (1992) and a book about her faith, _Quiet Strength_ (1994)
Her famous fingerprinting photo was taken in February 1956, when boycott leaders were arrested under an old anti-boycott law

trap.title: Woman, leader, or boycott?
trap.body: Several answer lines share this story. Claudette Colvin, a 15-year-old, refused to give up her seat on a Montgomery bus nine months before Rosa Parks did and later became a _Browder v. Gayle_ plaintiff. Martin Luther King Jr. led the boycott that Parks’s arrest started, and the Montgomery Bus Boycott itself is a separate answer, so listen for “this woman,” “this man,” or “this event.”
trap.fix: Parks clues: December 1, 1955, NAACP secretary, seamstress, the Highlander Folk School, James Blake, “tired of giving in,” and Detroit. Colvin clues: age 15, March 1955, and being a _Browder_ plaintiff. King clues: Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, the Montgomery Improvement Association, and “I Have a Dream.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Rosa Parks (or Rosa Louise McCauley Parks)
